'''Alexander Sergei Tuzhilin''' (born 1957) is a Professor of Data Science and Information Systems and the Leonard N. Stern Endowed Professor of Business at [[New York University]]'s [[Stern School of Business]]. He also serves as the Dean of Computer Science at the [[University of the People]] on the pro bono basis.

Professor Tuzhilin is known for his work on personalization, recommender systems, machine learning and AI, where he has made several contributions, including being instrumental in developing the area of Context-Aware Recommender Systems (CARS), proposing novel methods of providing unexpected and cross-domain recommendations based on the principles of deep-learning, developing novel approaches to customer segmentation, and discovery of unexpected patterns in data.

== Education ==
Tuzhilin received his B.A. in Mathematics from the [[New York University]] in 1980, M.S. in Engineering Economics from the Department of Management Science and Engineering at [[Stanford University]] in 1981, and Ph.D. in computer science from NYU's [[Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences]] in 1989, his doctoral advisor being Zvi Kedem.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.stern.nyu.edu/faculty/bio/alexander-tuzhilin|title=Alexander Tuzhilin|website=NYU Stern|language=en|access-date=2020-04-19}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Tuzhilin|first=Alexander|url=http://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~atuzhili/cv.pdf|title=CV|work=NYU Stern}}</ref>

== Career ==
Tuzhilin joined the faculty at the [[New York University Stern School of Business]] in 1989 as an Assistant Professor of Information Systems. He is currently the Leonard N. Stern Professor of Business. He is also the Dean of Computer Science at the University of the People.<ref><!--https://www.uopeople.edu/about/leadership-team/dr-alexander-tuzhilin-->Dr. Alexander Tuzhilin
Dean, Computer Science, University of the People</ref>

=== Research ===
Tuzhilin researches [[data mining]] in databases, [[personalization]], [[recommender system]]s, and [[customer relationship management]].<ref name=":1" />

In 2006, Tuzhilin was hired by Google and given access to its monitoring systems to do a study on [[click fraud]]. This was part of a class-action settlement requiring Google to offer advertisers up to $60 million in refunds. Tuzhilin concluded that defining and tracking click fraud will be difficult, because it is often not possible to decipher whether Web surfers were clicking on an advertising link out of malice or as part of an innocent online excursion.<ref><!--http://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/02/technology/02iht-click.2363792.html-->Search giants team up to combat 'click fraud', New York Times, August 2, 2006</ref><ref><!--http://articles.latimes.com/2006/jul/22/business/fi-click22-->Expert's Report Backs Google in Lawsuit Over Click Fraud, Los Angeles Times, July 22, 2006</ref><ref><!--http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/07/21/AR2006072101233.html-->Report: Google Tries to Fight Click Fraud, Washington Post, July 21, 2006</ref><ref><!--http://online.wsj.com/articles/SB116308638049018624-->So Many Hits, So Few Sales, Wall Street Journal, November 13, 2006</ref>

=== Patents ===
In 2001, Tuzhilin patented a method of building customer profiles and using them to recommend products and services. Tuzhilin said of the patent, 'It's very broad and very general, and occupies some prime real estate in this space. It essentially covers technologies that are crucial for implementation of customer relationship management.' He added that the patent was careful not to stipulate that the technology was designed for Internet applications. Others pointed out that there were legal exceptions to business methods patents. Any individuals or companies that can show they have been engaged in a business practice for at least a year before a patent application for that practice was filed may be able to circumvent the patent.<ref><!--http://www.nytimes.com/2001/07/30/business/patents-method-collecting-consumer-data-renews-questions-about-patents-business.html-->A method of collecting consumer data renews questions about patents on business practices, New York Times, July 30, 2001</ref>

In March 2012, Yahoo sued Facebook for violating 10 of its patents. Facebook countersued Yahoo, claiming that it violated Facebook patents that covered 80% of the Yahoo's 2011 revenues. Three of Facebook's patents were originally granted to Tuzhilin.<ref><!--http://dealbook.nytimes.com/2012/04/03/facebook-accuses-yahoo-of-infringing-on-patents/-->Facebook Accuses Yahoo of Infringing on Patents, New York Times, April 3, 2012</ref><ref>[https://techcrunch.com/2012/04/04/yahoo-vs-facebook/ How Facebook’s Winning The War Against Yahoo], Patent By Patent, TechCrunch, Apr 4, 2012</ref><ref><!--http://blogs.ft.com/tech-blog/2012/04/how-facebook-built-its-legal-defence-against-yahoo/-->How Facebook built its legal defence against Yahoo, Financial Times, Apr 03 2012</ref>
